title: The Birth of Venus
about: About the year 1485, in the Florence of the Medici, Sandro Botticelli painted the goddess of love as she comes ashore, newly born of the sea. The winds blow her toward the land upon a scallop shell, and an attendant hastens to cover her with a flowered cloak. He worked in tempera upon canvas, a rare thing in that city of panel painters, and touched the hair and the leaves with gold. Her pose was borrowed from the statues of the ancients. Little noticed for three centuries, the picture is now the glory of the Uffizi.

title: Primavera
about: In an orange grove where it is always spring, Venus stands beneath her son while the Three Graces dance and Mercury stirs the clouds with his staff. Botticelli painted the scene in tempera on a great panel about 1480, most likely for a young kinsman of Lorenzo de' Medici. No one has fully explained its meaning, and perhaps that is part of its hold. Botanists have counted hundreds of plants in the meadow, each drawn from life. At the right the west wind seizes a nymph, and she becomes Flora, scattering roses. It hangs in the Uffizi.

title: Mona Lisa
about: Leonardo began this portrait in Florence about 1503, and it is held to show Lisa Gherardini, wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo. He never delivered it. The panel travelled with him into France, and he was still refining it in his last years. There are no hard outlines here; the corners of the mouth and eyes dissolve in thin veils of shadow, the manner the Italians call sfumato, and so the expression seems to change as one looks. Stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and recovered two years later, it returned the most famous painting on earth.

title: Annunciation
about: Leonardo was scarcely past twenty, and still at work in the shop of Andrea del Verrocchio, when he painted the angel Gabriel kneeling before the Virgin in a walled Tuscan garden. The picture dates from the 1470s and came to the Uffizi in 1867 from a monastery outside Florence. Already the young painter goes his own way: the angel's wings are those of a real bird, and the far mountains melt into blue haze. Look also for the flowers in the grass, each one studied. For many years the work was credited to other hands.

title: The Last Supper
about: On the end wall of a friars' dining hall in Milan, Leonardo set down the moment when Christ tells the twelve that one of them will betray him. He laboured at it from about 1495 to 1498 for Duke Ludovico Sforza. Wishing to work slowly, he painted in tempera and oil upon dry plaster rather than in true fresco, and the surface began to flake within his own lifetime. Every line of the room runs to the head of Christ. The wall stood when bombs destroyed much of the refectory in 1943, and it may still be visited there.

title: The School of Athens
about: Pope Julius II summoned the young Raphael to Rome and gave him the walls of his private library to paint. Between 1509 and 1511 he filled one of them with the philosophers of the ancient world, gathered beneath a mighty vault. Plato points to the heavens and Aristotle holds his hand above the earth. Tradition says that Plato wears the face of Leonardo, and that the brooding figure on the steps is Michelangelo, then at work in the chapel nearby. Raphael himself looks out from the far right. The fresco remains where he painted it, in the Vatican.

title: Bacchus and Ariadne
about: Abandoned on the island of Naxos, Ariadne turns from the departing ship of Theseus and beholds the god Bacchus, who leaps from his chariot at the sight of her. Titian painted the meeting between 1520 and 1523 for Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, who wanted a private chamber hung with tales from the ancient poets. Cheetahs draw the chariot, and in the sky above Ariadne shines the crown of stars into which the god will change her diadem. The blue of that sky is costly ultramarine. Since 1826 the canvas has belonged to the National Gallery in London.

title: The Hunters in the Snow
about: Three hunters come home over the hill with their dogs, and they have little to show for the day: a single fox. Below them the valley lies frozen, and the villagers skate upon the ponds. Bruegel painted the panel in 1565 for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jonghelinck, as one of a series on the seasons of the year, of which five remain. It was a time of bitter winters in the Low Countries. Mark the inn sign hanging by one hook and the magpie crossing the cold air. The picture has long been among the treasures of Vienna.

title: Netherlandish Proverbs
about: Here is a village where every person acts out a saying. One man beats his head against a brick wall; another casts roses before swine; a third carries daylight out in a basket. Bruegel painted the panel in 1559, and scholars have found in it more than a hundred proverbs of the Low Countries, many still in use. A globe hangs upside down upon the wall of the inn, the sign of a world turned on its head. The picture is at once a game and a sermon on human folly. It is kept in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin.

title: The Peasant Wedding
about: The feast is held in a barn at harvest time, with sheaves stacked to the rafters. The bride sits quietly before a green cloth, a paper crown above her head, while two men carry in bowls of porridge on a door taken from its hinges. Bruegel painted the scene about 1567, near the end of his short life, and those who knew of him said he liked to go among country people at their fairs and weddings. Which guest is the bridegroom has never been settled. The panel passed into the Habsburg collections and remains in Vienna.

title: The Harvesters
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: It is high summer, and the wheat stands taller than the men who cut it. Some labour still with their scythes; others have gathered beneath a pear tree to eat bread and porridge, and one lies fast asleep. Bruegel painted this panel in 1565 as part of the same cycle of the seasons that holds The Hunters in the Snow. Nothing sacred or princely is shown, only work, rest and the wide country falling away to the sea, and in that it was something new. The Metropolitan Museum in New York acquired the picture in 1919.

title: Children's Games
about: A whole town has been given over to children. They roll hoops, walk on stilts, ride barrels, play leapfrog and blind man's buff, and no grown person is anywhere to be seen. Bruegel painted the panel in 1560, and patient observers have named some eighty different games among more than two hundred small figures. He looked down on the square from a height, as he often did, so that nothing should be hidden. Whether he meant simple delight or a quiet word about the folly of mankind, no one can say. The painting hangs in Vienna.

title: The Tower of Babel
about: The tower climbs through the clouds and is already giving way, for it leans upon its hill and the lower storeys crumble while the upper are yet unbuilt. Bruegel painted the panel in 1563, the year he moved from Antwerp to Brussels, and he gave his tower the tiers of the Colosseum, which he had seen in Rome ten years before. King Nimrod inspects the masons in the lower corner. Cranes, treadwheels and scaffolds are drawn with a builder's exactness, and the ships in the harbour are no larger than insects beside it. The picture is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

title: Winter Landscape with Skaters and a Bird Trap
museum: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels
about: A Brabant village lies under snow, and its people have come out upon the frozen river to skate, to spin tops and to play at curling. The small panel is dated 1565. Under the tree at the right a heavy door has been propped on a stick, with grain scattered beneath it to tempt the birds, and some have read in this a warning that the skaters stand in no less danger on the ice. The composition was so loved that the painter's descendants and followers copied it more than a hundred times. It hangs in Brussels.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
about: No one knows for whom Hieronymus Bosch painted this triptych, nor exactly when; it is placed between about 1490 and 1510, and a traveller saw it in a palace at Brussels in 1517. At the left God presents Eve to Adam. In the centre a multitude sports among giant birds and fruit, and at the right the night of hell receives them. Whether the middle panel shows a lost paradise or a warning against pleasure is still disputed. King Philip II of Spain acquired the work and sent it to the Escorial. It has hung in the Prado since 1939.

title: Feast of the Rosary
about: In 1506 Albrecht Dürer was living in Venice, and the German merchants of that city asked him for an altarpiece for their church of San Bartolomeo. He painted the Virgin crowning the Emperor with roses while the Child crowns the Pope, with the whole of Christendom kneeling round. The Venetians had thought him only an engraver; this panel, he wrote home, silenced them. He stands at the right beneath a tree, holding a paper with his name. A century later the Emperor Rudolf II bought the picture and had it carried over the Alps to Prague, where it remains.

title: The Large Piece of Turf
about: A clod of meadow, dug up and looked at from the level of a beetle: dandelion, plantain, yarrow and common grasses, each rendered leaf by leaf. Dürer made this watercolour in Nuremberg in 1503, when no painter thought a patch of weeds a fit subject for art. The seeming disorder is carefully composed, and the pale blank ground lets every blade stand clear. He held that art lies hidden within nature, and that he who can draw it out possesses it. The sheet is among the most prized possessions of the Albertina in Vienna, and is seldom shown.

title: The Night Watch
about: The civic guardsmen of Amsterdam commissioned a group portrait for their banqueting hall, and in 1642 Rembrandt gave them something no one had seen before: a company on the move. Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, in black with a red sash, gives the order to march, and his lieutenant in yellow steps out beside him. A girl in gold, lit like a lamp, carries a fowl at her belt, its claws the emblem of the company. The scene is not set at night; old varnish darkened it and gave it the name. It is the pride of the Rijksmuseum.

title: The Syndics of the Drapers' Guild
about: Five officials of the Amsterdam cloth guild, whose duty was to judge the quality of dyed wool, look up from their book as though someone had just entered the room. Rembrandt painted them in 1662. He was in his middle fifties, bankrupt and out of fashion, yet he made of this routine commission the last and greatest of his group portraits. The table is seen from below, for the canvas was to hang high upon a wall. X-rays show how often he shifted the figures before he was content. The painting is in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

title: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
about: This is the only seascape Rembrandt ever painted. It dates from 1633, soon after the young master had come to Amsterdam, and shows the disciples struggling with their boat while Christ, wakened from sleep, prepares to calm the waves. Count the figures and there are fourteen: among the twelve the painter has set himself, one hand upon his cap, looking straight out of the picture. In March of 1990 thieves cut the canvas from its frame in the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. It has not been seen since, and the empty frame still hangs upon the wall.

title: View of Delft
about: Johannes Vermeer lived all his days in Delft and painted his native town from across the harbour about 1660, on a morning after rain. The near buildings lie in the shadow of a cloud; beyond them the sun strikes the tower of the New Church and a few red roofs. He laid small dots of thick paint upon the boats to make them glitter. Vermeer died in debt and was all but forgotten for two centuries. The Dutch state bought this canvas in 1822 for the Mauritshuis, and the novelist Marcel Proust called it the most beautiful painting in the world.

title: The Little Street
about: Two houses of worn brick, a woman sewing in a doorway, a maid bending over a barrel in the passage, and two children at play upon the pavement. Vermeer painted this corner of Delft about 1658, and nothing happens in it at all. The quiet is the subject. He set down the cracks in the masonry and the stains of whitewash as faithfully as another painter would record a face. In 2015 a study of the old tax registers of the town proposed that the site was the Vlamingstraat, where his aunt lived. The painting is in the Rijksmuseum.

title: The Milkmaid
about: A kitchen maid pours milk into an earthen bowl, and the thin stream seems the only thing moving in the world. Vermeer painted her about 1660. Light falls from the window at the left across the bread upon the table, where he has scattered points of bright paint to give the crust its sparkle. On the bare wall he took the trouble to paint a nail and the holes left by others. X-rays show that he first put a rack of jugs behind her, then took it away. The Dutch state bought the picture for the Rijksmuseum in 1908, lest it be sold abroad.

title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
about: She turns over her shoulder as though someone had spoken her name. This is no portrait of a known sitter, but what the Dutch called a tronie: a study of a head, a costume and an expression. Vermeer painted it about 1665 and wound the turban in ultramarine, a pigment ground from lapis lazuli. The pearl is made of scarcely more than two strokes, a bright touch above and the soft reflection of the collar below. In 1881 the neglected canvas fetched little more than two guilders at a sale in The Hague. It now hangs in the Mauritshuis.

title: The Art of Painting
about: A painter sits at his easel with his back to the viewer, and before him a young woman poses as Clio, the Muse of History, with her trumpet and her book. Vermeer painted this allegory of his own calling in the later 1660s and kept it by him until he died; his widow tried in vain to save it from his creditors. On the wall hangs a map of the Netherlands, creased and gleaming, and a heavy curtain is drawn aside as if to admit a visitor. The canvas has belonged to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna since 1946.

title: The Garden of Love
about: Elegant couples have gathered before a garden pavilion, and cupids tumble among them with torches, doves and garlands. Rubens painted the canvas about 1633. He had lately married Helena Fourment, a bride of sixteen when he was fifty-three, and many have thought her features return among the ladies here. The scene was something new, a celebration of courtship in modern dress, and the painters of French garden parties a century later would look back to it. King Philip IV of Spain hung the picture in his bedchamber. It is now in the Prado in Madrid.

title: A View of Het Steen in the Early Morning
about: In 1635 Peter Paul Rubens, rich in honours and weary of courts, bought the manor of Het Steen between Brussels and Antwerp. He painted this wide view of it about a year afterwards, for his own pleasure and not for sale. The sun has just risen at the right. A cart sets off for market, a fowler stalks partridges behind a bush, and the flat fields of Brabant run on to a far horizon where a town may be made out. He joined many boards to make so broad a panel. It is in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Supper at Emmaus
about: Two disciples have walked the road with a stranger and sat down with him at an inn. He blesses the bread, and in that instant they know him for the risen Christ. Caravaggio painted the scene in Rome in 1601 for the nobleman Ciriaco Mattei. One disciple thrusts out his arms, so that his hand seems to break the surface of the picture; the other grips his chair, his elbow coming through a torn sleeve. A basket of fruit stands at the very edge of the table, ready to fall. The canvas is in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Cardsharps
about: A well-dressed youth studies his hand of cards and suspects nothing. Behind him an older rogue peers over his shoulder and signals with two fingers, while the young cheat reaches for a card tucked in his belt. Caravaggio painted this scene of the Roman streets about 1594, when he was poor and unknown, and it made his name: Cardinal Francesco del Monte bought it and took the painter into his household. It was copied again and again. The original vanished in the 1890s and came to light in 1987. It hangs in the Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth.

title: Basket of Fruit
about: A wicker basket stands at the very edge of a ledge, heaped with grapes, figs, a peach, a pear and an apple in which a worm has made its hole. Some of the vine leaves are already dry and curling. Caravaggio painted it in Rome about 1599, when Italian painters seldom thought fruit alone worth a canvas. Cardinal Federico Borromeo of Milan owned the picture and prized it; he wrote that he had sought a companion for it and found none its equal. He gave it to the Ambrosiana, the library and gallery he founded, where it remains.

title: Las Meninas
about: In a high room of the palace at Madrid the little Infanta Margarita stands among her maids of honour, her dwarfs and a sleepy dog. Velázquez, painter to King Philip IV, has put himself at the left before a huge canvas, brush in hand. The mirror on the far wall reflects the king and queen, who must therefore stand where the beholder stands. He painted it in 1656. Seen close, the dresses dissolve into loose strokes; from a distance they turn to silk. The red cross of Santiago upon his breast was added after he was knighted. It hangs in the Prado.

title: The Surrender of Breda
about: In 1625 the Dutch fortress of Breda yielded to the armies of Spain after a long siege. Ten years afterwards Velázquez painted the scene for the Hall of Realms in the new Buen Retiro palace at Madrid. The Dutch commander, Justin of Nassau, offers the key of the town, and the victor Ambrogio Spinola lays a hand upon his shoulder to keep him from kneeling. It is a picture of courtesy more than of conquest. The upright pikes of the Spanish gave it its other name, Las Lanzas. The canvas hangs in the Prado.

title: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners)
about: Women spin and wind wool in the shadows of a workshop, and one wheel turns so fast that its spokes have vanished. Beyond them, in a lighted alcove, fine ladies stand before a tapestry. For a long time the painting was taken for a plain scene of the royal tapestry works in Madrid. It is now read as the fable of Arachne, the weaver who dared to challenge the goddess Minerva and was turned into a spider. Velázquez painted it in his last years, about 1655 to 1660. Strips were later added to the canvas. It hangs in the Prado.

title: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede
about: A stone mill rises above the river Lek under a sky heavy with cloud, and three women walk the road in a gleam of sun. Jacob van Ruisdael painted it about 1670, and it has become the very image of the Dutch countryside. The mill was a real one; its foundations may still be seen in the town of Wijk bij Duurstede. He took liberties all the same, lowering the horizon so that the mill might stand like a tower against the weather. More than half the canvas is sky. The painting is in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

title: The Laughing Cavalier
about: He is not laughing, and no one knows that he was a cavalier. An inscription gives only his age, twenty-six, and the year, 1624, when Frans Hals of Haarlem painted him with one hand on his hip and a look of perfect self-possession. The sleeve is embroidered with arrows, flaming horns and lovers' knots, the emblems of courtship. In 1865 the Marquess of Hertford bought the portrait at auction in Paris for many times its estimate, outbidding a Rothschild, and the affair made it famous. The popular title came later. Wallace Collection, London.

title: The Stonemason's Yard
about: This is not the Venice of the festivals. Canaletto painted it about 1725, early in his career, looking across a small square on the Grand Canal where masons were dressing stone, most likely for the rebuilding of a nearby church. A woman draws water from a well, another spins at a window, and a child has tumbled over in the foreground while his mother rushes toward him. Across the water stands the church of Santa Maria della Carita, whose bell tower fell down in 1744. Many hold it to be his masterpiece. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Entrance to the Grand Canal, Venice
about: The great domed church of Santa Maria della Salute stands at the mouth of the Grand Canal, built by the Venetians in thanksgiving after the plague of 1630. Canaletto painted the view about 1730, when English gentlemen on the Grand Tour were carrying his pictures home by the dozen as records of the city they had seen. He often used a ruler and compasses for his buildings, and then set the water alive with small curved strokes for the ripples. Gondolas and cargo boats go about their business in the morning light. The canvas is in Houston.

title: Piazza San Marco
about: This is among the earliest views of Venice by the young Canaletto, who had begun as a painter of stage scenery beside his father. It can be dated to about 1723 by a small circumstance: the great square is being repaved, and the new pattern of white stone has been laid on one side only. The basilica and its bell tower stand in a strong, stormy light, and ragged awnings shelter the market stalls. His later views are brighter and smoother, made for travellers. This one has the drama of the theatre. It hangs in Madrid.

title: Seaport with the Embarkation of Saint Ursula
about: According to the old legend, the British princess Ursula sailed on pilgrimage with eleven thousand maidens, and all were martyred on the journey home. Claude Lorrain, a Frenchman who spent his working life in Rome, painted their departure in 1641. The saint stands on the steps at the left with her banner, yet the true subject is the morning sun upon the harbour, which lays a path of light across the water and warms the columns of the portico. Painters studied his manner of placing the sun within the picture for two hundred years. It belongs to the National Gallery, London.

title: Seaport with the Embarkation of the Queen of Sheba
about: The Queen of Sheba descends the palace steps at sunrise to take ship for Jerusalem and the court of King Solomon. Claude painted the canvas in Rome in 1648 for the Duc de Bouillon, a general in the service of the Pope. As always with him, the story is small and the light is everything: the sun stands low over the sea and gilds each ripple. J. M. W. Turner so honoured this picture that he left two of his own to the nation on condition they hang beside Claude's. The National Gallery in London has kept that bargain.

title: The Avenue at Middelharnis
about: A straight road lined with thin, lopped trees runs from the eye to a village in the province of South Holland, and a man with a dog comes walking toward the viewer. Meindert Hobbema painted it in 1689. He had by then given up painting for a living and held a post gauging wine casks for the city of Amsterdam, so that this, his best-known work, is a late and solitary one. At the right a gardener tends his nursery of young trees. The plunging perspective has been a lesson to painters ever since. It hangs in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Courtyard of a House in Delft
about: A maidservant leads a little girl by the hand down the steps of a small paved yard. Through the archway beside them another woman stands in the passage, looking out toward the street. Pieter de Hooch painted the scene in 1658 in Delft, where he worked for some years in the same quiet town as Vermeer. The stone tablet above the arch came from a cloister of the town, and still exists. Every brick is given its due, and the sunlight on the far wall is the true event of the picture. National Gallery, London.

title: Dresden from the Right Bank of the Elbe below the Augustus Bridge
about: Bernardo Bellotto was the nephew and pupil of Canaletto, and carried his uncle's art north of the Alps. In 1748, as court painter to the Elector of Saxony, he recorded Dresden from across the river: the dome of the Frauenkirche, the long stone bridge, and the Catholic court church, its tower still under construction. The cool, exact light is his own. Two centuries later the city was destroyed by bombing in 1945, and this prospect is still known there as the Canaletto view, for Bellotto too went by his uncle's name. The painting hangs in the Old Masters Gallery in Dresden.

title: View of Vienna from the Belvedere
about: Driven from Dresden by war, Bernardo Bellotto came to Vienna in 1759 and stayed two years in the service of the Empress Maria Theresa. He painted this prospect of the city from the upper palace of the Belvedere, which Prince Eugene of Savoy had built as his summer residence. The formal gardens descend toward the town; the green dome of the Karlskirche rises at the left and the spire of Saint Stephen's cathedral in the centre. The Viennese still call this the Canaletto view, and cite the picture when the skyline is in dispute. Kunsthistorisches Museum.

title: The Maas at Dordrecht
about: In July of 1646 a great fleet and an army of thirty thousand men were assembled at Dordrecht, and Aelbert Cuyp, a native of the town, recorded the scene a few years later. Small boats carry dignitaries out to a large ferry, where drums beat and an officer is received. Yet what remains in the memory is the light, a soft gold laid across the wide river in the early morning. Cuyp never travelled to Italy, and learned that radiance from the pictures of countrymen who had. The canvas is in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

title: Et in Arcadia Ego (The Arcadian Shepherds)
about: Shepherds in a golden country have come upon a tomb, and one of them traces with his finger the words cut in the stone: Et in Arcadia ego. The words are commonly taken for the voice of Death, present even in Arcadia. Nicolas Poussin painted the canvas in Rome about 1638, and gave the scene the calm of an ancient relief; the stately woman at the right lays her hand upon a shepherd's shoulder as if to steady him. The shadow of the kneeling man's arm falls across the stone like a sickle. The picture hangs in the Louvre.

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
about: Four figures dance in a ring with their backs to one another while old Father Time plays the lyre. They are thought to stand for Poverty, Labour, Wealth and Pleasure, the round that human fortune travels again and again. Poussin painted the picture in Rome in the 1630s for Giulio Rospigliosi, who later became Pope Clement IX and who is said to have devised the subject. Above the dancers the chariot of the Sun crosses the sky, and a child at the side blows bubbles that will not last. It hangs in the Wallace Collection, London.

title: Rain, Steam and Speed - The Great Western Railway
about: A locomotive comes headlong out of the weather across Maidenhead Bridge, its firebox glowing through the rain. Turner exhibited the picture in 1844, when he was nearly seventy and the railways were scarcely older than a child. Brunel's bridge over the Thames had been finished only five years before. Nothing in the painting has an edge; bridge, river and sky are swept into one veil of gold and grey. Look closely before the engine and a hare may be found running on the track, the swiftest of creatures about to be overtaken. The canvas is in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Fighting Temeraire
about: The Temeraire had fought beside Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar in 1805. In 1838, her service long over, she was towed up the Thames to Rotherhithe to be broken up for timber, and Turner made of that last journey an elegy for the age of sail. The old warship is pale as a ghost; the steam tug before her is dark and full of fire, and the sun sets behind them both. He was in his sixties, and never consented to sell the picture, which he called his darling. It came to the nation at his death and hangs in the National Gallery.

title: Dido Building Carthage
about: Queen Dido, in blue and white at the left, oversees the raising of her new city on the African shore, and the sun climbs above the river in a haze of gold. Turner exhibited the canvas in 1815 and thought it his finest work; he refused great sums for it and once spoke of being buried wrapped in it. It is his open challenge to Claude Lorrain, the painter he most revered. By the terms of his will it hangs to this day in the National Gallery beside Claude's seaport, that the world may judge between them.

title: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth
about: Sea, snow and smoke turn about a single point, and at the centre a paddle steamer labours with her mast bent like a bow. Turner showed the picture in 1842, and afterwards told how he had the sailors lash him to the mast for four hours that he might observe such a storm; whether the tale is true has long been doubted, for he was then sixty-seven. A critic dismissed the work as soapsuds and whitewash, and the old man was wounded by it. It is now held one of his greatest, and belongs to Tate Britain.

title: Ulysses Deriding Polyphemus
about: Ulysses has blinded the one-eyed giant and escaped from his cave, and now stands on his gilded ship beneath a scarlet banner, taunting his enemy as the sails are raised. The giant writhes on the mountain above, half lost in cloud. Turner exhibited the canvas in 1829, soon after his first long stay in Italy, and the sunrise blazes with a colour he had not dared before. In the dawn the horses of the sun god may faintly be seen rising, and sea nymphs sport about the prow. John Ruskin called it the central picture of his career. National Gallery, London.

title: The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons
about: On the night of 16 October 1834 fire broke out in the old Palace of Westminster and consumed the Houses of Parliament. Turner was among the thousands who crowded the banks of the Thames to watch, and he filled sketchbooks with what he saw. The next year he exhibited this canvas, in which the flames lean across the river and turn the water to brass, while Westminster Bridge stands white and enormous at the right. He is said to have finished it on the walls of the gallery in a few hours before the public came. It is in Philadelphia.

title: Norham Castle, Sunrise
about: Norham Castle stands above the river Tweed on the border of England and Scotland. Turner first drew it as a young man in 1797 and returned to the subject throughout his life; it is told that he once took off his hat to the ruin as he passed, saying it had made his fortune. This canvas dates from about 1845. The castle is no more than a blue shadow in the mist, the sun a pale stain of yellow, and a cow stands drinking in the shallows. He never exhibited it. It came to the nation with his bequest and hangs at Tate Britain.

title: The Hay Wain
about: A farm wagon stands in the shallows of the river Stour on a summer noon, near the mill that the painter's father owned in Suffolk. Constable painted the great canvas in his London studio in 1821, from sketches he had made in the country of his boyhood; the cottage at the left belonged to a neighbour, Willy Lott. It found no buyer at the Royal Academy. Three years later it was shown in Paris, where the King of France awarded it a gold medal and the painters marvelled at its fresh, broken greens. It hangs in the National Gallery.

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds
about: John Fisher, Bishop of Salisbury, was a friend to Constable, and asked him for a view of the cathedral from his own garden. The painter finished it in 1823 and set the bishop himself in the corner at the left, pointing out the spire to his wife with his cane. Two elms bend together to frame the building like a doorway. The bishop liked everything but the dark cloud over the spire, and requested a sunnier sky in a second version. This first one is in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows
about: Constable painted this canvas in 1831, in the years of grief that followed the death of his wife, Maria. A storm is passing over the cathedral. Lightning strikes near the roof, a wagon crosses the swollen river, and a rainbow arches over all and comes to rest upon the house of his friend, Archdeacon John Fisher. He counted it the work that would best show posterity what he had attempted, and he went on retouching it for years. In 2013 it was bought for the British nation, and it belongs to Tate.

title: Wivenhoe Park, Essex
about: In the late summer of 1816 Major-General Francis Slater-Rebow asked Constable to paint his country seat near Colchester. The fee was welcome; it helped the painter to marry Maria Bicknell that autumn after a courtship of seven years. He worked out of doors and had to widen the canvas with added strips at either side to take in everything his patron wished to see. The general's young daughter drives a donkey cart at the far left, and fishermen draw a net across the lake. The picture is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

title: Flatford Mill (Scene on a Navigable River)
about: Barges are being worked up the river Stour toward the mill at Flatford, which the painter's father owned. A boy sits astride the tow-horse while another unhitches the rope so that the boat may pass beneath the bridge. Constable painted the scene in 1816 and 1817, largely in the open air, which was then a rare practice for so large a canvas. He scratched his signature into the foreground as if written in the earth with a stick. These few miles of Suffolk, he said, had made him a painter. The picture belongs to Tate Britain.

title: Hadleigh Castle
museum: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
about: A ruined tower stands above the mouth of the Thames on the morning after a night of storm. Constable had sketched the place in 1814. He took up the drawing again and exhibited this large canvas in 1829, a few months after his wife Maria died of consumption, leaving him with seven children. The paint is rough and flecked with white, laid on with the knife, and the broken tower is often read as an image of his own desolation. Far out over the estuary the light is returning. It is at the Yale Center for British Art.

title: Chain Pier, Brighton
about: Constable took his family to Brighton in the 1820s in the hope that sea air would mend his wife's failing health. He did not care for the town, which he called Piccadilly by the seaside, yet he walked its beach daily with his sketch box. This large canvas, shown in 1827, sets the fashionable new pier in the distance and gives the foreground to fishermen, their boats and anchors, beneath a sky of driving cloud. It is his only large picture of a seaside resort. The pier was destroyed by a storm in 1896. Tate Britain.

title: Stonehenge
about: Constable visited Stonehenge once only, in 1820, and made a careful pencil drawing of the stones. Fifteen years later, near the end of his life, he worked that drawing up into this watercolour and showed it at the Royal Academy in 1836. Over the ancient circle he set a double rainbow against a sky of black storm, and a hare starts away in the corner. He wrote for it a caption on the mystery of the monument, standing remote upon a bare and boundless heath. The sheet is in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
about: A man in a dark green coat stands upon a crag with his back turned and looks out over a world of mist, through which the peaks rise like islands. Caspar David Friedrich painted the canvas in Dresden about 1818. He assembled the view in his studio from separate drawings made in the sandstone mountains along the Elbe. The wanderer's face is not shown, and so each beholder takes his place. Little regarded at the painter's death, the picture has become the emblem of the Romantic age. It hangs in the Kunsthalle at Hamburg.

title: The Sea of Ice
about: Slabs of pack ice have been driven one upon another into a jagged pyramid, and at the right the stern of a crushed ship can just be seen. Friedrich painted the scene in 1823 and 1824, moved by accounts of the voyages then seeking a passage through the Arctic. He had never been to the far north; he studied the ice breaking up on the river Elbe at Dresden. The picture found no buyer and was still in his studio when he died in 1840. Its cold shattered forms seem to belong to a later century. It hangs in Hamburg.

title: The Monk by the Sea
about: One small figure stands upon a pale strip of shore before a dark sea and an immense sky. There is nothing else. Friedrich worked on the canvas from 1808 to 1810 and, as examination has shown, painted out the ships he had first set upon the water, leaving emptiness itself for his subject. Those who saw it in Berlin in 1810 were shaken; the poet Heinrich von Kleist wrote that it was as though one's eyelids had been cut away. The young crown prince of Prussia urged its purchase. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie.

title: The Stages of Life
about: On a Baltic shore at evening five people watch five ships come in. The old man with his back turned is taken to be the painter himself, and the others his nephew, his children and a daughter grown; the vessels answer to them, the farthest still upon the open sea and the nearest lowering her sails for harbour. Friedrich painted the picture about 1835, the year a stroke began to rob him of the strength to work in oils. The two small children hold up a Swedish flag, for he was born a Swedish subject. It hangs in Leipzig.

title: Two Men Contemplating the Moon
about: Two friends have halted on a forest path at night to look at the sickle moon and the evening star beside it. The elder, in a cape, is thought to be the painter; the younger, leaning on his shoulder, his pupil August Heinrich. Friedrich painted the small canvas in 1819 and 1820. The men wear the old German costume which the authorities of the day had forbidden as a badge of political dissent, and he is said to have joked that the pair were plotting. An uprooted oak clings to the slope beside them. The picture is in Dresden.

title: The Lonely Tree
about: An old oak stands alone in a wide green plain, its crown dead and its lower boughs still in leaf, and a shepherd leans against the trunk while his flock grazes. Mountains close the distance under the morning cloud. Friedrich painted the canvas in 1822 for the Berlin banker and collector Joachim Heinrich Wagener, as the companion to an evening scene, Moonrise over the Sea. Ponds lie in the meadows, a village spire shows among the trees, and the whole has a peace uncommon in his art. The two pictures remain together in the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

title: Moonrise over the Sea
about: Three figures, two women and a man, sit together upon a great rock at the edge of the Baltic and watch the moon come up behind a bank of violet cloud. Two sailing ships are gliding home. Friedrich painted the canvas in 1822 as the evening companion to The Lonely Tree, which shows the morning. The watchers have their backs turned, as so often with him, that the eye may look with them and not at them. Some have read the returning ships as lives nearing their end. The picture hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

title: The Great Enclosure near Dresden
about: The Great Enclosure was a tract of low meadow beside the Elbe, a little to the north-west of Dresden. Friedrich painted it about 1832, at the hour after sunset when the sky still burns yellow and the earth has gone dark. The river has drawn back and left shallow channels of water that hold the last light, and a single barge drifts with its sail spread. The horizon is gently bowed, as if the eye could feel the roundness of the world. It is among the last of his great landscapes and hangs in Dresden.

title: The Parasol
about: A young woman sits on a bank with a fan in her hand and a little dog asleep in her lap, while her companion shades her face with a green parasol. Francisco Goya painted the canvas in 1777, at thirty-one, as the pattern for a tapestry to be woven at the royal manufactory in Madrid. The hanging was meant for a place above a window in the dining room of the heir to the throne, and so the group is built as a pyramid and seen from below. Nothing of his later darkness is here. It hangs in the Prado.

title: The Meadow of San Isidro
about: On the fifteenth of May the people of Madrid crossed the river Manzanares to keep the feast of their patron, Saint Isidore, with picnics on the grass. Goya painted the holiday in 1788: parasols, carriages, a white multitude on the slopes, and beyond the water the long skyline of the city, with the royal palace and the great dome of San Francisco. It is only a small sketch for a tapestry that was never woven, for the king died that winter and the project was abandoned. Goya admitted the subject had cost him much labour. Museo del Prado.

title: Liberty Leading the People
about: For three days in July of 1830 the people of Paris fought at the barricades and drove King Charles X from his throne. Eugène Delacroix had taken no part. If he had not fought for his country, he wrote to his brother, he would at least paint for her, and that autumn he made this picture. Liberty strides over the stones with the tricolour in one hand and a musket in the other, a workman, a student and a street boy beside her. The towers of Notre-Dame show through the smoke. The state bought the canvas and then kept it long from view. Louvre.

title: Mr and Mrs Andrews
about: Robert Andrews and Frances Carter were married in November of 1748, and their lands were joined. Not long afterward the young Thomas Gainsborough, born in the same Suffolk town of Sudbury, painted the couple beneath an oak on their estate, with the harvest stooked beside them. He was about twenty-three. The sitters occupy one side only; the rest is given to their well-kept fields beneath a changing sky. A patch on the lady's lap was left unfinished and no one knows what it was to hold. The picture stayed with the family until 1960. National Gallery, London.

title: A Burial at Ornans
about: In the autumn of 1848 a funeral was held at Ornans, the small town in eastern France where Gustave Courbet was born. He painted it on a canvas more than six metres wide, and asked the townspeople themselves to pose: the priest, the mayor, the gravedigger, his own sisters and friends, some fifty in all. Such a scale had been kept for kings and saints. When it hung in Paris at the Salon of 1850 the critics found the mourners ugly and the subject beneath notice. Courbet said it was in truth the burial of Romanticism. It is in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: The Meeting (Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet)
about: On a country road near Montpellier the painter, with his pack and staff, meets his patron Alfred Bruyas, who has come out with his servant and his dog to greet him. Courbet painted the scene in 1854, soon after he arrived as the banker's guest. Bruyas doffs his hat; the servant bows his head; the painter merely lifts his chin and his pointed beard. When it was shown in Paris the next year the wits renamed it Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet, and mocked its vanity. Bruyas left his collection to the Musée Fabre in Montpellier, and there it hangs.

title: The Cliff at Étretat after the Storm
about: In the summer of 1869 Gustave Courbet took a house by the sea at Etretat, on the coast of Normandy, where the chalk has been worn into arches and needles. He painted the great cliff in the washed light that follows rain, with fishing boats drawn up on the shingle and no living figure in sight. Rock, water and sky are each laid on in a different manner, much of it with the knife. The canvas was acclaimed at the Salon of 1870. Within a year came war, the Commune, his imprisonment and at last his exile. Musée d'Orsay.

title: The Gleaners
about: Three women stoop in a stubble field to gather the ears of wheat that the harvesters have left behind, a right the poorest of the village had held since ancient times. Far off, in the sunlight, the great stacks rise and an overseer sits his horse. Jean-Francois Millet was a farmer's son from Normandy, and he lived among the peasants of Barbizon. When he showed the picture in 1857, well-to-do visitors took alarm at it and spoke of revolution. He gave the three bent figures the gravity of statues. It hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: The Angelus
about: At dusk in a potato field near Barbizon a man and a woman have laid down their fork and basket and bow their heads, for the bell of the distant church is ringing the evening prayer. Millet painted the picture between 1857 and 1859, remembering how his grandmother had made the family stop work in the fields to say the Angelus for the dead. The American who ordered it never came to collect it. Thirty years later it was sold for a fortune, and it became the most reproduced painting of its century. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

title: The Bridge at Narni
about: In 1825 the young Corot went to Italy with an allowance from his father, a Paris cloth merchant, and stayed three years. In September of 1826 he sat down above the river Nera at Narni, in Umbria, and painted the ruined bridge of the Emperor Augustus in the open air. The light of morning is on the broken arch and the sandy bed of the stream. It is only a study in oil on paper, never meant for exhibition. From it he made a formal picture for the Salon. The sketch is in the Louvre.

title: Souvenir de Mortefontaine
about: A woman reaches up into a slender tree by the edge of a lake while two children gather flowers at its foot, and a great leaning tree shelters the other side of the picture. All is veiled in the silver mist of early morning. Camille Corot painted it in 1864, at sixty-seven, not from nature but from remembrance of the ponds at Mortefontaine north of Paris, which he had often visited. He was by then the most admired landscape painter in France. The Emperor Napoleon III bought the picture from the Salon, and it is in the Louvre.

title: Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks
about: According to the legend, the Sultan of Turkey in 1676 demanded the submission of the Cossacks who lived beyond the rapids of the Dnieper, and they sent him back a letter of magnificent abuse. Repin shows them composing it, each man contributing an insult and roaring at his own wit. He worked on the canvas for eleven years, from 1880 to 1891, travelling in Ukraine to collect faces, weapons and dress, and using his friends for models. Tsar Alexander III bought it for thirty-five thousand roubles. It hangs in the Russian Museum.

title: Barge Haulers on the Volga
about: Eleven men in harness drag a laden barge upstream against the current, under a hot sky. Ilya Repin was a student of twenty-six when he travelled to the Volga in 1870 and lived for a summer among such labourers, drawing them one by one; the leader, Kanin, had once been a priest. He finished the canvas in 1873. Each man is a separate character, weary or sullen or resigned, and only the fair-haired boy at the centre lifts his head and pulls against the strap. The picture made Repin's name. Russian Museum, Saint Petersburg.

title: Impression, Sunrise
about: From a hotel window at Le Havre, the port where he had grown up, Claude Monet painted the harbour at daybreak in 1872: a red sun, its broken reflection, and two small boats dark upon the grey water. He worked fast, in thin strokes that scarcely cover the canvas. When it was shown in Paris in 1874 a mocking critic seized on the title and called the whole company of painters Impressionists, and the name remained. Thieves carried the picture off from the Musée Marmottan in 1985; it was found five years later and returned to its wall.

title: Water Lilies
about: In the garden he had made for himself at Giverny, Claude Monet set his easel beside the pond and looked down. This canvas is dated 1906. There is no bank in it, no horizon and no sky save the one that lies reflected among the lily pads, so that depth and surface become one. He was in his middle sixties, and would paint this water for twenty years more, growing ever harder to please; some canvases he slashed and burned before they could be shown. The pale clouds drift beneath the blossoms. The picture belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: Garden at Sainte-Adresse
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: In the summer of 1867 Monet was twenty-six, penniless, and staying with his aunt at Sainte-Adresse on the Normandy coast. He painted his family taking the air on a terrace above the Channel; the old gentleman seated in the foreground is his father. Two flags snap in the wind, the gladioli burn red, and steamers and sailing ships crowd the horizon. The high viewpoint and the flat bands of terrace, sea and sky owe something to the Japanese prints he had begun to collect. The Metropolitan Museum bought the canvas in 1967 with the help of its friends.

title: Woman with a Parasol - Madame Monet and Her Son
about: On a windy summer day in 1875, near Argenteuil, Monet painted his wife Camille and their son Jean upon a rise of meadow, seen from below against the sky. It was the work of a single sitting out of doors, done in a few hours. Her veil and skirt are swept by the same quick strokes as the clouds, and the grass throws a yellow light up on her arm. The boy was then eight. Camille would die four years later at thirty-two. The canvas was shown at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876 and is now in Washington.

title: The Magpie
about: A single magpie sits on a wattle gate, and the low sun casts the shadow of the fence across the snow. Monet painted the scene near Etretat in Normandy in the hard winter of 1868 to 1869, standing out in the cold to do it. The shadows are not grey but blue, a truth of the eye that few painters had yet dared to set down. The jury of the Paris Salon refused the picture in 1869. It is now reckoned among the finest snow scenes ever made, and it is one of the best-loved works in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Poppy Field
about: A mother and child come down through the long grass of a summer field, and another pair follows over the brow of the hill. The poppies are no more than dabs of red, larger in the foreground than nature would allow. Monet painted this in 1873 at Argenteuil, a small town on the Seine near Paris, where he had settled with his family after the war with Prussia; the figures are most likely his wife Camille and their son Jean. He showed it the following year at the first Impressionist exhibition. It hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: La Grenouillère
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: La Grenouillère was a floating cafe and bathing place on the Seine at Croissy, an easy train ride from Paris. In the summer of 1869 Monet and his friend Renoir set up their easels there side by side. Monet was so poor that he had at times no money for paint. To catch the shiver of the water he laid down broad, separate strokes of black, ochre and blue, and in doing so found the method that would be called Impressionism. The little round island was known to its patrons as the Camembert. The canvas is in the Metropolitan Museum.

title: San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk
about: Monet came to Venice only once, in the autumn of 1908, at the age of sixty-seven, and he lamented that he had not come when he was younger and bolder. He stayed two months with his wife Alice and began some three dozen canvases. Here the island church of San Giorgio Maggiore stands dark against a sky that passes from orange through gold to deep blue. Alice died in 1911, and he finished the Venetian pictures in his studio at Giverny while in mourning. The Welsh collector Gwendoline Davies bought this one, and by her bequest it came to Cardiff.

title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
about: At the start of 1877 Monet took a small flat near the Gare Saint-Lazare, the Paris terminus he knew from his journeys to Normandy, and obtained leave to paint inside the station. He made twelve views in a few months. Steam was his real subject: it rises blue and white beneath the iron and glass roof and dissolves the engines, the travellers and the distant houses alike. He showed several of the series at the third Impressionist exhibition that spring, where the novelist Emile Zola praised them. This canvas belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: Bridge over a Pond of Water Lilies
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: Monet bought land beside his house at Giverny in 1893, diverted a stream to make a pond, and built across it an arched footbridge in the Japanese manner. He said he had planted the lilies for pleasure and without a thought of painting them. In the summer of 1899 he made twelve views of the bridge from one spot, of which this is one. The span crosses the canvas from edge to edge above water crowded with leaves and flowers, and no sky is seen. He was fifty-eight. The picture is in the Metropolitan Museum, New York.

title: The Houses of Parliament, Sunset
about: Monet loved London for its fog. In the winters from 1899 to 1901 he worked from a terrace of St Thomas's Hospital across the Thames, painting the towers of Westminster late in the afternoon as the sun went down behind them. He kept many canvases going at once and changed from one to another as the light altered. This one, dated 1903, was finished from memory in his studio at Giverny. The building is a blue shadow without detail; the fire is all in the sky and the river. It belongs to the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

title: Haystacks, End of Summer
about: In the fields near his house at Giverny the farmers piled their wheat in tall thatched stacks to await threshing. Monet began to paint them in the late summer of 1890 and went on through the winter, working on several canvases at once and changing from one to the next as the hour passed. He wished to show not the stacks but the light that lay over them. Fifteen of the series were exhibited in Paris in May of 1891 and nearly all were sold within days. This one, dated 1891, hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Bal du moulin de la Galette
about: On Sunday afternoons the working people of Montmartre came to dance in the garden of an old windmill at the top of the hill. In 1876 Renoir rented a studio nearby and painted the scene, with his friends posing for the dancers and the talkers at the table. Sunlight falls through the acacias in round patches upon straw hats and striped dresses, and some critics complained that the figures looked spotted. The painter Gustave Caillebotte bought the canvas and left it to the French nation at his death. It is one of the glories of the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Luncheon of the Boating Party
about: The meal is over, and a company of friends lingers on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on the Seine at Chatou. Renoir painted them in 1880 and 1881. The young woman at the left, playing with a little dog, is the seamstress Aline Charigot, whom he would later marry; the man in the straw hat astride a chair at the right is his fellow painter Gustave Caillebotte. Bottles, glasses and fruit upon the white cloth make a still life in themselves. Duncan Phillips bought the picture in 1923, and it hangs in Washington.

title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
about: A young woman in a scarlet hat sits with a small girl on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise, the riverside restaurant at Chatou where Renoir set his Luncheon of the Boating Party. He painted them in the spring of 1881. They were not sisters; the elder was a young actress named Jeanne Darlot, and the title was the dealer's invention. A basket of coloured wool stands before them like a painter's palette, and the river shines through the blossoming trees behind. The canvas was shown at the Impressionist exhibition of 1882 and came to Chicago in 1933.

title: La Grenouillère
about: In the summer of 1869 Renoir and Monet painted side by side at La Grenouillère, a bathing place and floating cafe on the Seine west of Paris. Both were young and often hungry; Renoir carried bread from his parents' table to his friend. Each made the same view of the little round island with its single tree, where the Parisians gathered in their Sunday clothes. Renoir's strokes are softer and more feathery than Monet's, and he gives more notice to the people and their dress. From such afternoons Impressionism was born. This canvas is in the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.

title: Pont Neuf, Paris
about: From an upper window of a cafe by the Seine, Renoir looked down upon the oldest bridge in Paris at midday, crowded with carriages, soldiers, hawkers and strollers. He painted it in 1872, when he was thirty-one and sold almost nothing. His brother Edmond told how he was sent down to the pavement to stop passers-by with idle questions, so that the painter might have a moment to set them down; Edmond himself is seen twice, with a straw hat and a cane. The shadows are blue and the light is everywhere. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

title: The Ballet Class
about: The lesson is drawing to its end. An old ballet master leans on his long stick and watches one dancer, while the others wait about the room, yawning, adjusting a ribbon, scratching a shoulder. Degas painted the canvas between 1871 and 1874 for the singer Jean-Baptiste Faure. The master is Jules Perrot, once a celebrated dancer. Degas haunted the rehearsal rooms of the Paris Opera for years, drawn less by the performance than by the labour behind it. The slanting floorboards hurry the eye to the far wall. The picture hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: A Cotton Office in New Orleans
about: Degas's mother was born in New Orleans, and in the autumn of 1872 he crossed the Atlantic to visit her family there. He painted his relations at their business: his uncle Michel Musson in the foreground testing a tuft of raw cotton, one brother reading the newspaper, another leaning idly at a window. The firm failed even as he worked upon the picture in 1873. Five years later the museum of the town of Pau in the Pyrenees bought the canvas, and so it became the first of his works to enter a public collection. It remains there.

title: Place de la Concorde
about: The Vicomte Ludovic Lepic, a friend of the painter, strides across the great square of Paris with a cigar in his teeth, his two daughters and their dog turning the other way. Degas painted the canvas in 1875. Figures are cut by the edge as in a photograph, and half the picture is given to empty paving, an arrangement no painter before him would have risked. The work disappeared in Germany at the end of the Second World War and was thought destroyed. In 1995 it was shown again, at the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg, where it remains.

title: The Dance Foyer at the Opera on the rue Le Peletier
about: In the rehearsal room of the old Paris opera house, a young dancer stands ready to begin while the ballet master, in white, raises his hand. The others stretch at the bar or rest along the wall. Degas painted this small canvas in 1872, and it is among the first of the ballet pictures that would occupy him for the rest of his life. An empty chair stands in the foreground, as if someone had only now risen from it. The building itself burned to the ground the following year. The painting is in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Boulevard Montmartre, Spring
about: Troubled in his later years by an ailment of the eye that kept him from working out of doors, Camille Pissarro took to painting from hotel windows. In February of 1897 he engaged a room in the Grand Hotel de Russie in Paris and through that spring painted fourteen views of the boulevard below in all weathers and at all hours. Here the plane trees are in new leaf and carriages stream toward the vanishing point. The canvas was taken from its Jewish owner in Germany in the 1930s, restored to his heirs in 2000, and sold in London in 2014.

title: The Boulevard Montmartre at Night
about: Of the fourteen views that Pissarro painted of the Boulevard Montmartre from his hotel window in 1897, this is the only one made after dark. Rain has fallen, and the wet street throws back the light of the shop fronts, the gas lamps and the new electric lights, each of a different colour. The cabs waiting along the kerb are a few dark strokes with a spark of yellow. He was then sixty-six. He never signed the canvas nor exhibited it during his life. It is in the National Gallery, London.

title: Hoar Frost
about: An old road climbs through ploughed fields near Pontoise on a morning of white frost, and a peasant goes up it with a bundle of sticks upon his back. Pissarro painted the scene in 1873. Long shadows of poplars that stand outside the picture fall across the furrows, and the earth is rendered in thick, dry touches of ochre, pink and blue. He showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, where one critic jeered that it was nothing but palette scrapings laid on a dirty canvas. It hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Flood at Port-Marly
about: In December of 1872 the Seine left its banks at Port-Marly, a village west of Paris, and the water stood in the street before the wine merchant's shop. Alfred Sisley, born in Paris of English parents, painted the scene without any sense of calamity: a grey mild sky, a punt, a few people going about their business. His father's firm had been ruined by the late war, and he now lived by his brush in real want. Four years later the river rose again and he returned to paint it. This canvas is in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

title: The Bridge at Villeneuve-la-Garenne
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: A suspension bridge of iron and stone, then not thirty years old, strides across the Seine to a village of white houses with coloured shutters. Sisley painted it in the summer of 1872. He set his easel low on the bank, so that the roadway of the bridge sweeps overhead, and laid the reflections on the water in short flat strokes of blue, green and cream. Holiday makers sit on the grass, and a boat is being rowed across. The dealer Paul Durand-Ruel bought the canvas that same year. It is in the Metropolitan Museum.

title: The Seine at Port-Marly, Piles of Sand
about: The Seine had to be dredged to keep its channel open for the barges, and the sand was heaped on the bank to be sold to builders. Sisley found the men at this work in 1875, standing in their narrow boats among the mooring poles, and made a picture of it. He was living close by at Marly-le-Roi. The river is a strong and unexpected blue, and the pale mounds in the foreground answer the white clouds. Of all the Impressionists he remained most faithful to landscape alone. The canvas is at the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
about: A young woman stands behind a marble counter set with champagne, beer and a dish of oranges, and looks out with an expression no one has been able to name. Behind her a great mirror shows the crowded music hall, and her own back, strangely displaced, with a gentleman in a top hat before her. Manet painted the picture in 1882, when he was gravely ill and could work only seated; a barmaid named Suzon came to pose in his studio. In the top corner hang the green boots of a trapeze artist. It was his last great work. Courtauld Gallery, London.

title: Music in the Tuileries
about: A fashionable crowd has gathered beneath the trees of the Tuileries garden in Paris to hear the band, which is nowhere to be seen. Manet painted the scene in 1862 and filled it with his acquaintance: the poet Baudelaire, the composer Offenbach, his own brother Eugene, and himself at the far left edge. The paint is laid on in abrupt patches, and the middle of the picture is scarcely more than a blur. When it was exhibited the following year one visitor threatened it with his walking stick. It is often called the first painting of modern life. National Gallery, London.

title: The Railway
about: A young woman sits before an iron fence with a book and a sleeping puppy in her lap and looks up from her page. Beside her a little girl in a white dress with a blue bow turns away to watch the steam rising from the tracks of the Gare Saint-Lazare. No train is to be seen. Manet painted the picture in 1873, in a friend's garden above the cutting; the model was Victorine Meurent, who had posed for him ten years before. The Salon accepted it in 1874 and the public was baffled. It is in Washington.

title: Monet Painting in His Studio Boat
about: Claude Monet had a boat fitted with a cabin and an awning, so that he might paint from the middle of the river. In the summer of 1874 Edouard Manet, staying across the Seine from Monet's house at Argenteuil, painted his younger friend at work in it, with Camille Monet seated in the doorway behind. Manet had always been a painter of the studio. That season, beside Monet, he worked in the open air with a lighter palette and a quicker touch, though he never consented to exhibit with the Impressionists. The picture is in Munich.

title: Summer's Day
about: Two young women are being rowed upon the lake of the Bois de Boulogne, the park on the western edge of Paris near which Berthe Morisot lived. One looks straight out; the other turns to watch the ducks. Morisot painted the canvas about 1879 and showed it at the Impressionist exhibition of the following year. Her brush moves in rapid zigzags, so that water, dresses and foliage seem all to tremble together. She exhibited with the group in seven of its eight shows, and was married to the brother of Edouard Manet. National Gallery, London.

title: The Harbour at Lorient
about: In the summer of 1869 Berthe Morisot went to stay with her sister Edma at Lorient in Brittany. The two had learned to paint together; Edma had lately married a naval officer and laid aside her brushes. Here she sits on the harbour wall beneath a parasol, at the edge of a wide and luminous view of quays and masts. Edouard Manet admired the picture so warmly when he saw it that Berthe made him a present of it. She was twenty-eight, and it was among the first works in which she found her own manner. Washington.

title: Mont Sainte-Victoire with Large Pine
about: The limestone mountain of Sainte-Victoire stands a few miles east of Aix-en-Provence, where Paul Cézanne was born and where he chose to live apart from the painters of Paris. He painted it again and again, in oil and in watercolour, to the end of his life. In this canvas of about 1887 the boughs of a pine in the foreground follow the outline of the far ridge, so that near and distant are locked together; a railway viaduct crosses the valley between. He gave the picture to the young poet Joachim Gasquet, who had admired it. It is in the Courtauld Gallery, London.

title: The Basket of Apples
about: Cézanne said that he wished to astonish Paris with an apple. He painted this still life about 1893, and nothing in it obeys the common rules. The table edge does not meet behind the cloth; the bottle leans; the basket tips forward, and the biscuits on their plate are seen from two heights at once. He looked at each thing separately and long, and set down every view. Painters of the next generation built a new art upon such liberties. The canvas is at the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: The Card Players
about: Two countrymen sit facing one another across a small table, a bottle between them, and study their cards. No one speaks. In the first half of the 1890s Cézanne painted five versions of the card game, using labourers from his family's estate near Aix as his models, and this is the smallest and the last, stripped of every onlooker. The man at the left with the pipe was a gardener there. The two figures lean inward like the halves of an arch. The picture hangs in the Musée d'Orsay; another version sold privately for a sum beyond all precedent.

title: The Gulf of Marseilles Seen from L'Estaque
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: L'Estaque was a fishing village on the bay west of Marseilles. Cézanne first went there in 1870 to keep out of the way of the war, and returned many times in the years that followed. He wrote to his friend Pissarro that the place was like a playing card, red roofs against the blue sea, and that the sun was so fierce that things stood out in flat silhouette. In this canvas of about 1885 the tiled houses, the water and the far hills are three firm bands, each built of small slanting strokes. Metropolitan Museum, New York.

title: Mont Sainte-Victoire
about: In 1902 Cézanne built himself a studio on the hill of Les Lauves, north of Aix-en-Provence. A short climb above it the whole plain opened before him, with the Mont Sainte-Victoire on the horizon, and there he painted the mountain again and again in his last years. The fields and trees have become patches of green, ochre and violet set side by side, and the sky is made of the same colours as the earth. In October of 1906 he was caught by a storm while painting out of doors, and he died a few days later. Philadelphia.

title: The Starry Night
museum: Museum of Modern Art, New York
about: In May of 1889 Vincent van Gogh entered the asylum of Saint-Paul at Saint-Remy in Provence of his own will. From his barred window he had watched the sky before sunrise, with the morning star very large, and in June he painted this night from memory by day. The village is partly invented, and its spire is more Dutch than Provencal. A cypress rises like a dark flame, and the heavens turn in great wheels of thick paint. He thought the picture a failure and scarcely mentioned it. Since 1941 it has belonged to the Museum of Modern Art.

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: During the summer of 1889, while he was a patient at the asylum of Saint-Remy, Van Gogh was allowed to work in the fields beyond its walls. The cypresses of Provence filled his thoughts; he wondered that no one had yet painted them as he saw them, and likened their form to an Egyptian obelisk. This canvas shows ripe wheat bending in the mistral beneath a sky of rolling cloud, with the blue Alpilles behind. He counted it among his best summer landscapes and made two further versions. It is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Wheatfield with Crows
about: Three paths run into a field of ripe wheat and none of them arrives anywhere. Above, a dark blue sky presses down, and a flock of crows scatters across it. Van Gogh painted this double-width canvas at Auvers-sur-Oise in July of 1890, in the last weeks of his life, and wrote of trying to express sadness and extreme loneliness in his pictures of the fields. It is often called his final work, though that is not certain, and others were painted after it. He shot himself on the twenty-seventh of that month. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

title: Irises
museum: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
about: Van Gogh began this picture in May of 1889, within the first week of his arrival at the asylum of Saint-Remy, working in the overgrown garden before he was permitted to go beyond the walls. He called painting the lightning conductor for his illness. Each flower is drawn with a firm contour, in the manner of the Japanese woodcuts he admired, and every one is different; a single white iris stands apart among the blue. His brother Theo sent the canvas to an exhibition in Paris that autumn. It now hangs in the Getty Museum in Los Angeles.

title: Café Terrace at Night
about: In September of 1888, at Arles in the south of France, Van Gogh carried his easel into the Place du Forum after dark and painted the terrace of a cafe by the light of its great gas lamp. He was delighted to make a night picture with no black in it, only blue, violet and green against sulphur yellow. This is the first canvas in which he set down his starry sky. The square is still shown to every visitor to Arles. The picture hangs in the Kröller-Müller Museum, in a forest park in the Netherlands.

title: Starry Night Over the Rhône
about: A short walk from the yellow house he rented at Arles, Van Gogh stood on the bank of the Rhone one night in September of 1888 and painted the river beneath the stars. The gas lamps of the town throw long golden reflections across the water, and overhead the Great Bear shines in a sky of deep blue-green. Two lovers walk in the foreground. He had long wished to paint the stars, which, he wrote, always set him dreaming. The canvas was shown in Paris the next year and is now in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Bedroom in Arles (third version)
about: In October of 1888, while he waited for Gauguin to join him in the Yellow House at Arles, Van Gogh painted his own bedroom. He wished the colour alone to speak of rest: pale violet walls, a bed of butter yellow, a scarlet coverlet. The first canvas was later damaged by damp. In September of 1889, at the asylum of Saint-Remy, he made two copies of it, and this smaller one was meant for his mother and sister in Holland. The pictures hanging above the bed differ in each. It is in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Almond Blossom
about: On the last day of January 1890 a son was born to Theo van Gogh in Paris and named Vincent after his uncle. The painter, still confined at Saint-Remy, was overjoyed, and set to work on a gift for the child's bedroom: branches of almond in flower against a blue sky, the earliest blossom of the southern spring. The bold outlines and the view from beneath recall the Japanese prints he loved. He fell ill before he could paint more of the kind. The family never parted with it, and it hangs in the Van Gogh Museum.

title: The Yellow House
about: In May of 1888 Van Gogh rented four rooms in the right wing of this house on the Place Lamartine at Arles, the corner with the green shutters. He dreamed of founding there a studio of the south where painters might live and work as brothers. In September he painted it under a sky of hard cobalt; a train crosses the viaduct at the right, and the restaurant where he took his meals is the pink building at the left. Gauguin came that October and stayed nine weeks. The house was damaged by bombing in 1944 and pulled down.

title: The Harvest
about: In June of 1888 Van Gogh worked for a week in the wheat fields of the plain of La Crau outside Arles, under a burning sun, until a storm put an end to the harvest. This wide view he judged the best of the campaign, saying that it killed everything else he had done. A blue cart stands at the centre; around it are ricks, ladders, a reaper and gleaners, and the ruined abbey of Montmajour shows on its hill at the left. The colours are laid in flat, clear zones. The canvas hangs in the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

title: The Night Café
museum: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven
about: Van Gogh stayed awake for three nights in September of 1888 to paint the all-night cafe at Arles where he lodged, sleeping by day. The walls are blood red, the ceiling green, and four lamps burn with haloes of orange above a billiard table that casts its shadow on the yellow floor. A few drunkards and vagrants slump at the tables, and the landlord stands in white. He meant, he wrote, to show a place where a man could ruin himself or go mad, and he gave the canvas to the landlord against his debt. It is at Yale.

title: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
about: Paul Gauguin painted this, his largest canvas, in Tahiti at the end of 1897, on coarse sacking, in a month of feverish work. He was sick, in debt, and had lately learned of the death of his daughter Aline. It is to be read from right to left: a sleeping infant, a figure reaching up for fruit, and at last an old woman near death, with a blue idol presiding over all. He said afterwards that he had meant it for his testament and had then gone into the hills to end his life. It is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

title: Tahitian Women on the Beach
about: Gauguin had been a stockbroker in Paris, with a wife and five children, before he gave up everything to paint. In 1891 he sailed for Tahiti in search of a life untouched by Europe, and this is among the first pictures he made there. Two women sit upon the sand. One wears the flowered wrap of the island; the other, the long pink dress the missionaries had brought. The colours lie flat and unshadowed, bounded by dark outlines. Neither woman meets the eye, and their thoughts are their own. The canvas hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

title: Arearea (Joyousness)
about: Two women sit beneath a tree, and one of them plays a flute. Behind, others dance before a great idol, and across the foreground walks a dog of bright orange. Gauguin painted the canvas in 1892, during his first stay in Tahiti, mingling what he saw with what he imagined of the old religion of the island. When it was shown in Paris the following year the red dog was much derided. He thought the picture among his best, and bought it back himself when his works were auctioned in 1895. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
about: For two years Georges Seurat laboured on this great canvas of Parisians taking their ease on an island in the Seine. He made dozens of drawings and oil sketches on the spot, then built the picture in his studio out of small separate touches of colour, trusting the eye to blend them. The figures stand as still as carvings. It was shown in 1886 at the last Impressionist exhibition and caused an uproar. He was twenty-six. Later he added the painted border of dots. Since 1926 the picture has belonged to the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: Bathers at Asnières
about: Working men and boys rest on the bank of the Seine at Asnieres, a suburb of Paris, on a hot afternoon; the chimneys of the factories at Clichy smoke in the distance. Seurat was twenty-four when he finished this, his first great canvas, in 1884. The jury of the official Salon refused it, and he showed it instead with a new society of independent artists. He later went back and added dots of colour here and there, as on the boy's orange hat. Across the water lies the island of La Grande Jatte. National Gallery, London.

title: Grand Canal, Venice
about: Paul Signac was a yachtsman as well as a painter, and he liked to arrive at a harbour by sea. In the spring of 1904 he spent some weeks in Venice and filled his notebooks with watercolours. From them he composed this canvas in his studio the following year. The domes of Santa Maria della Salute float in a haze of rose and gold, and the gondolas and mooring posts are set down in small blocks of pure colour, like the cubes of a mosaic. After the early death of his friend Seurat he had become the leader of their school. Toledo, Ohio.

title: The Pine Tree at Saint-Tropez
museum: Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow
about: In 1892 Signac sailed his boat into the small fishing port of Saint-Tropez, then unknown to fashion, and liked it so well that he took a house there. He stayed for the better part of twenty years. This umbrella pine, painted in 1909, spreads its crown across the whole canvas in strokes of orange, violet, green and blue, none of them blended. The Moscow merchant Ivan Morozov, one of the boldest collectors of the age, bought the picture. His collection was taken by the state after the revolution, and it now hangs in the Pushkin Museum.

title: The Bonaventure Pine
