about: A single great pine fills the picture, its dark canopy spread like a cloud above the bay of Saint-Tropez, where small sails pass in the distance. Signac painted it in 1893, the year after he first came to that coast. Every part is built of separate dots, according to the method he had worked out with Georges Seurat: blue and violet in the shade, orange and yellow in the sun, left for the eye to mingle. The tree is given the dignity of a portrait. The canvas is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

title: At the Moulin Rouge: The Dance
about: The Moulin Rouge opened in Montmartre in 1889, and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was at his table there almost nightly. In this large canvas of 1890 the dancer known as Valentin the Boneless, a tall thin man in a top hat, leads a young woman through the steps of the quadrille while the crowd looks on. A lady in pink crosses the foreground. The painter was the heir of an ancient noble house, crippled in boyhood, and he found his subjects among the entertainers of the night. The owner of the dance hall bought the picture and hung it there. Philadelphia.

title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
about: A gentleman and a lady share an umbrella at a crossing of the new boulevards near the Gare Saint-Lazare, and the wet paving stones shine. Gustave Caillebotte painted this immense canvas in 1877, when he was twenty-eight, and showed it at the third Impressionist exhibition. He was a man of means, an engineer by training, and he drew the plunging lines of the streets with care; the lamp post divides the picture in two. Long forgotten after his early death, it was bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1964 and is among its best-known works.

title: Boating on the Yerres
about: The family of Gustave Caillebotte owned a country house at Yerres, south-east of Paris, with a park running down to the river. In the summers of the 1870s he painted the oarsmen and bathers there. These narrow, flat-bottomed canoes, driven by a double paddle, were then a new amusement. He shows them from above and behind, gliding into the picture, with the green of the trees broken up in the water. Caillebotte was himself an expert boatman and later designed racing yachts. He showed the canvas with the Impressionists in 1879. Milwaukee Art Museum.

title: The Sleeping Gypsy
museum: Museum of Modern Art, New York
about: A wandering woman lies asleep on the desert sand, her mandolin and water jar beside her, and a lion has come to sniff at her shoulder. The moon is full and the beast does not devour her. Henri Rousseau, a retired clerk of the Paris toll service who had taught himself to paint, showed the picture in 1897 and offered it to his native town of Laval, which declined. It then vanished for a quarter of a century and was found again in 1923. Every outline is sharp and still, as in a dream. It is in New York.

title: Tiger in a Tropical Storm (Surprised!)
about: A tiger crouches in the long grass with bared teeth while the rain slants down and lightning splits the sky. This is the first of the jungle scenes for which Henri Rousseau is remembered, shown in Paris in 1891. He liked it to be thought that he had served in Mexico as a soldier; in truth he never left France, and found his tropics in the hothouses of the Paris botanical garden and in illustrated books. The streaks of rain are laid over the whole in thin, translucent strokes. The picture is in the National Gallery, London.

title: The Kiss
about: A man bends to kiss a woman who kneels at the edge of a flowered meadow, and both are wrapped in one mantle of gold. Gustav Klimt painted the square canvas in Vienna in 1907 and 1908, laying real gold leaf and silver over the oil paint. His father had been a goldsmith's engraver, and he had lately seen the Byzantine mosaics of Ravenna. The man's robe is patterned with upright rectangles, the woman's with circles and flowers. The Austrian state bought the picture before it was even finished, and it hangs in the Belvedere palace.

title: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
about: Adele Bloch-Bauer was the wife of a Viennese sugar magnate and kept a salon where the artists and writers of the city gathered. Klimt worked three years upon her portrait and completed it in 1907. Only her face, shoulders and hands are painted as flesh; all the rest is a field of gold and silver leaf set with eyes, spirals and tiny squares. The picture was seized from the family after the German annexation of Austria in 1938. In 2006, after a long suit at law, it was restored to her niece, and it now hangs in New York.

title: Farm Garden with Sunflowers
about: Klimt spent his summers on the Attersee, a lake in the Austrian hills, rising early, rowing, and painting landscapes for his own pleasure. He painted this cottage garden about 1907 in the village of Litzlberg. There is no sky and no path; sunflowers, dahlias, asters and phlox press forward and fill the square canvas from edge to edge, like a tapestry. He is said to have used a small frame of cardboard to choose his view, and so his landscapes have no horizon. The picture hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna.

title: Poppy Field
about: Each summer Gustav Klimt left Vienna for the Attersee, a lake in the Upper Austrian hills, and painted landscapes there for his own delight. This meadow dates from 1907. The horizon is pushed almost to the top of the square canvas, and all below is a close weave of green touched with red poppies and white daisies, so that the fruit trees can scarcely be told from the grass. He took something from the French painters of the dot, and more from his own love of ornament. The picture hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna.

title: The Scream
about: Edvard Munch told how he was walking at sunset along a road above the fjord at Kristiania, as Oslo was then called, when the sky turned red as blood. His friends walked on; he stood trembling and felt a great scream pass through nature. In 1893 he set the memory down in tempera and crayon on cardboard. The figure has no age and no sex, and the lines of the sky run on through its body. In one of the red streaks he wrote in pencil that only a madman could have painted it. The picture is in the National Museum, Oslo.

title: The Girls on the Bridge
about: Three girls lean on the rail of a jetty and look down into the water, in the pale light of a northern summer night. Behind them stand a white house, a great linden tree and its dark reflection, and a small yellow moon. The place is Åsgårdstrand, a village on the Oslo fjord where Edvard Munch bought a fisherman's cottage and spent many summers. He painted this first version about 1901 and returned to the subject again and again over the next thirty years. It is one of the calmest of his pictures. National Museum, Oslo.

title: The Sun
about: In 1908 Munch suffered a collapse and spent eight months in a clinic at Copenhagen. He came home to Norway resolved to paint in a clearer and stronger key, and settled at Kragerø on the southern coast. There he made this sunrise over the skerries, its rays driving outward across rock and sea in bands of pure colour. It is the centre of the cycle he painted for the ceremonial hall of the university in Oslo, won in competition and unveiled in 1916 after years of dispute. It remains upon the end wall of that hall.

title: Four Trees
about: Four chestnut trees stand in a row before a range of low hills, and behind them the setting sun burns through bands of red and violet cloud. Three are still in leaf; the fourth is almost bare. Egon Schiele painted the canvas in the autumn of 1917, while he was serving as a soldier clerk in Vienna, and it has a stillness rare in his work. He was known chiefly for his unsparing drawings of the human body. A year later the influenza carried him off at twenty-eight, three days after his wife. Belvedere, Vienna.

title: Setting Sun
about: Two frail young trees, nearly leafless, stand on a dark slope above a cold sea. Beyond them lie islands the colour of rose and slate, and the sun has already sunk out of sight. Schiele painted the picture in 1913, at twenty-three, the year after he had spent some weeks in prison on account of his drawings. He often spoke of autumn trees as if they were persons, and these have the thinness of his own figures. The canvas belongs to the Leopold Museum in Vienna, which holds the largest collection of his work.

title: Ophelia among the Flowers
about: Until he was past fifty Odilon Redon worked almost wholly in black, in charcoal and lithograph, and peopled his sheets with creatures from dreams. Then he turned to colour, and his pastels bloomed. This one, made between about 1905 and 1908, began as an upright study of flowers in a vase. He turned the paper on its side, and the bouquet became a bank of blossoms above the stream where Ophelia, from Shakespeare's Hamlet, drifts with closed eyes. The traces of the vase may still be found. The National Gallery in London acquired it in 1977.

title: Composition VII
about: Wassily Kandinsky had been a lecturer in law at Moscow before he gave up the university at thirty to become a painter in Munich. He believed that colour acts upon the soul as music does, without need of any subject. For this, the largest and most intricate of his canvases, he made more than thirty studies in drawing, watercolour and oil; then, in November of 1913, he painted the whole in four days. Scholars find in its turmoil the themes of the Deluge, the Last Judgement and the Garden of Eden. It hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: Composition VIII
museum: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
about: Ten years lie between this painting and the storm of Composition VII, and the whole manner has altered. Kandinsky had returned from Russia to Germany and in 1922 joined the teaching staff of the Bauhaus at Weimar, where he taught the properties of form and colour. Here circles, triangles, straight lines and arcs are set upon a pale ground with the clarity of a diagram, and a dark disc with a glowing rim hangs in the upper corner. He painted it in 1923. Solomon Guggenheim bought it from the artist a few years later, and it is in New York.

title: Yellow-Red-Blue
about: Kandinsky painted this large canvas at Weimar in the spring of 1925, in the last months before the Bauhaus school removed to Dessau. It reads as an argument between two natures. On the left all is yellow, bright, straight-edged and clear; on the right a deep blue circle is crossed by a black winding line; and red holds the ground between them. He was then writing his treatise on point, line and plane, and the picture sets out its teaching. His widow Nina gave the work to the French nation in 1976. Centre Pompidou, Paris.

title: Cat and Bird
museum: Museum of Modern Art, New York
about: The face of a cat fills the whole picture, wide-eyed and watchful, and upon its forehead sits a small bird. The bird is not in front of the cat but within it: it is what the cat is thinking of. The nose is a red heart. Paul Klee painted this in 1928 while he was a master at the Bauhaus in Dessau, where he taught for ten years. He kept cats all his life and held that art does not reproduce the visible but makes visible. The picture is in the Museum of Modern Art, New York.

title: Castle and Sun
about: A city is built of nothing but small squares, oblongs and triangles of colour, set together like a child's blocks, and over it hangs a round orange sun. Paul Klee painted the picture in 1928, during his years as a teacher at the Bauhaus. He was the son of a music master and himself a fine violinist, and he composed his colours as intervals and rhythms. A journey to Tunisia in 1914 had first shown him, as he wrote in his diary, that colour and he were one. The painting is in private hands.

title: Evening; The Red Tree
about: An old apple tree twists against the dusk, its trunk and boughs a burning red and the air about it a deep blue. Piet Mondrian painted it between 1908 and 1910, when he was already near forty and known in Holland as a painter of quiet meadows and mills. The work of Van Gogh and of the bolder French colourists had lately opened his eyes. He kept only two colours and set them against each other at full strength. From this tree, by slow degrees, he would arrive at his pictures of pure line. Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

title: The Gray Tree
about: It is the same apple tree that Mondrian had painted in red and blue, and almost everything has been taken from it. In the autumn of 1911 he saw the Cubist pictures of Picasso and Braque shown in Amsterdam, and within months he had left Holland for Paris. Here the colour is drained to grey; the branches have become a web of curved strokes that spreads to every edge, and the spaces between them count for as much as the wood. A few years more and the tree would vanish altogether. Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

title: The Yellow Cow
museum: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
about: A yellow cow kicks up her heels and leaps across a landscape of blue, red and orange hills. Marc painted her in 1911. In his private scheme of colour, yellow stood for the female principle, gentle, cheerful and sensual, and the picture has been connected with his marriage that year to the painter Maria Franck. The blue triangle of the mountains behind may stand for himself. He wished to paint the world not as a man sees an animal, but as the animal feels itself to be. The canvas is in the Guggenheim Museum, New York.

title: The Large Blue Horses
about: Three blue horses bend their heads together, and the curves of their backs are repeated in the red hills behind them. Franz Marc painted the canvas in 1911, the year he founded the Blue Rider group in Munich with his friend Kandinsky. He had come to feel that animals were purer than men and closer to the spirit of creation, and he gave each colour a meaning: blue, he wrote, was the male principle, severe and spiritual. He was killed by a shell at Verdun in 1916, at thirty-six. The painting is in Minneapolis.

title: Lady in a Green Jacket
about: In the autumn of 1913 August Macke took his wife and small sons to live at Hilterfingen, on the shore of Lake Thun in Switzerland. The eight months he spent there were the happiest and most fruitful of his life. Here a woman in a green jacket stands with lowered head among autumn trees, while two couples stroll toward the water. The faces are left blank, and the figures are simply shapes of clear colour set in the sun. He was killed in France in September of 1914, in the second month of the war, at twenty-seven. Museum Ludwig, Cologne.

title: Zoological Garden I
about: Gentlemen in bowler hats stroll among the cages, and a bright parrot and a gentle deer look out from the foreground. August Macke loved zoological gardens and returned to them often with his sketchbook; for him they were a glimpse of Eden, where men and animals shared one peaceful world. He painted this canvas in 1912. The forms are broken into facets of colour, a manner he had lately learned from the modern painters of Paris and Italy, yet nothing in it is harsh. It is in the Lenbachhaus in Munich.

title: Garden on Lake Thun
about: Tree, path, wall and mountain have become so many glowing planes of red, blue, green and yellow, fitted together like panes of coloured glass. August Macke painted the garden in 1913 at Hilterfingen on Lake Thun, where he was living with his family. The French painter Robert Delaunay had shown him how colour alone can make space and light. The following April he travelled to Tunisia with his friend Paul Klee, and by autumn he lay dead on the Western Front. The canvas is in the art museum of Bonn, the city where he grew up.

title: Isle of the Dead (third version)
about: A small boat glides over still water toward an island of rock, where tall cypresses stand among tombs cut in the cliff. In the boat are an oarsman, a figure wrapped in white, and a coffin. The Swiss painter Arnold Böcklin made the first version at Florence in 1880 for a young widow who had asked for a picture to dream by, and he repeated it four times; this, the third, dates from 1883. He gave no explanation, and the title came from his dealer. Prints of it once hung in half the parlours of Germany. Berlin.

title: Lake Geneva from Chexbres
about: From the vineyards of Chexbres, high above the northern shore, Lake Geneva lies spread out like a great oval. Ferdinand Hodler painted the prospect several times, and this version dates from 1905. He was born poor in Bern, lost his parents and all his brothers and sisters to consumption, and rose to be the foremost painter of Switzerland. He believed that nature is ruled by repetition and symmetry, and so the clouds here march in an even row above the far mountains, and the near bank answers the curve of the distant one. Kunstmuseum Basel.

title: Lake Thun, Symmetric Reflection
about: The mountains on either side of Lake Thun slope down to the water, and the water gives them back again, so that the picture is divided along its middle like a folded sheet. Hodler painted it in 1909. He had a name for the principle he found everywhere in nature, the repeating of like forms, and called it parallelism. Here he strips the scene to pale blues and violets, with outlines as firm as those of a map, and lets a band of cloud lie across the peaks. The stillness is absolute. The canvas is in Geneva.

title: Spring in the Alps
museum: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
about: A farm woman leads two great horses across a high plateau, and behind her a sower casts his seed into the dark furrows. Snow still lies on the peaks. Giovanni Segantini painted the scene in 1897 near the village of Soglio in the Swiss mountains, for an American patron. Orphaned and unschooled, he had climbed ever higher in search of clearer light, and he laid his colours in long separate threads that make the air itself shine. Two years later he died in a hut on a mountain above the Engadine, aged forty-one. Getty Museum, Los Angeles.

title: Return from the Woods
about: At the close of a winter day a woman drags a sledge loaded with wood along a track toward her village. The snow is blue with evening, the church tower stands against the white slope, and one or two windows are already lit. Segantini painted the picture in 1890 at Savognin, in the Swiss canton of Graubunden, where he lived for eight years among the mountain farmers. He shows their toil without complaint and without sweetness. The canvas is kept in the museum built in his memory at St. Moritz.

title: The Ninth Wave
about: Sailors of old believed that the waves of a storm come in sequence, and that the ninth is the most terrible. Ivan Aivazovsky, born in the Crimean port of Feodosia, painted this vast canvas in 1850, when he was thirty-three. A ship has gone down in the night; her survivors cling to a broken mast as the great wave rises over them. Yet the sun is breaking through, warm and golden, and it is a picture of hope. He painted the sea from memory, never from life, and with astonishing speed. It hangs in the Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg.

title: The Black Sea
about: There is no shore in this picture, no wreck and no sunset; only dark water heaving under a heavy sky, and far off a single sail. Aivazovsky painted it in 1881, when he was sixty-four and had spent a lifetime producing brilliant effects of moonlight and storm. Here he put them all aside. The painter Ivan Kramskoi, a severe judge, wrote that it held nothing but sky and water, yet the water was a boundless ocean, and that he knew of no grander picture of the sea. The canvas hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: View of Constantinople and the Bosphorus
about: Aivazovsky first saw Constantinople in 1845, sailing with a Russian naval expedition, and the city on its strait never left his imagination. He went back many times, and several sultans honoured him and bought his work. In this canvas of 1856 the sun goes down behind the minarets of a mosque on the waterfront, and ships, caiques and the crowd on the quay are bathed in one amber light. He painted, as always, from memory, far from the place itself. The picture was sold at auction in London in 2012 and is privately owned.

title: Among the Waves
about: Aivazovsky was eighty-one when he painted this immense canvas in 1898, and it is said that he finished it in ten days. There is no ship in it, no wreck, no shore; only the grey-green sea rising under storm clouds, and a single shaft of light breaking through. He had painted some six thousand pictures in his long life, and many hold this the finest. He never sold it. With the rest of his gallery he left it to Feodosia, the Crimean town where he was born and where he died two years later.

title: Morning in a Pine Forest
about: Mist still hangs between the pines, and the first sun touches the tops of the trees. About a fallen trunk in the clearing a she-bear and her three cubs are clambering. Ivan Shishkin, who knew the forests of Russia tree by tree, painted the canvas in 1889; the bears were put in by his friend Konstantin Savitsky. Both men signed it. The collector Pavel Tretyakov bought the picture and had Savitsky's name removed, judging the work to be Shishkin's in conception. It became the best-known painting in Russia, printed even on the wrappers of chocolates. Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: Rye
about: A cart track runs through a field of ripe rye, and great pines stand along it like sentinels under a sky that promises thunder. Shishkin painted the picture in 1878, from studies made the summer before near Yelabuga on the river Kama, the town of his birth. On a sketch for it he wrote of expanse, of open space, of rye, the grace of God and the wealth of Russia. Swallows skim low over the grain, and one of the pines is dead, bare among the living. The canvas hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

title: Rain in an Oak Forest
about: A summer shower is passing through the oak wood. The far trees dissolve in wet mist, puddles shine on the path, and a couple pick their way along it beneath a single umbrella, with a third walker a few paces ahead. Ivan Shishkin painted the picture in 1891. He was famed for the exactness of his trunks and leaves, and some thought him too literal; here he shows that he could paint the air between the trees as well. The whole is held in a soft silver grey. The canvas hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: Winter
about: Deep snow lies in a pine forest, loading every bough and burying the fallen trunks. Nothing moves; a single small bird sits on a branch. Shishkin painted the canvas in 1890 and limited himself almost to white, brown and a cold grey-blue, yet the drifts have weight and the distance has depth. He had studied the forest in every season for forty years, and his fellow painters called him its tsar. Eight years later he died seated at his easel, with a new canvas just begun. Russian Museum, Saint Petersburg.

title: Oak Grove
about: Old oaks stand in the full blaze of a summer noon, and their shadows lie sharp on the grass. Shishkin painted this large canvas in 1887, after years of drawing and painting such trees one by one. Every furrow of the bark is there, and every cluster of leaves, yet the eye takes in the whole grove at once, and feels the heat. He taught his pupils to study nature with the patience of a scientist. The oak, strong and long-lived, stood in his mind for Russia itself. The picture is in Kyiv.

title: Evening Bells
about: The domes of a monastery glow in the last sun across a quiet bend of river, and one seems to hear its bells over the water. A ferry crowded with pilgrims is putting out from the far bank, and two empty boats lie moored in the foreground. Levitan painted the canvas in 1892. No such monastery exists; he put it together from memories of several he had seen on the upper Volga and near Zvenigorod. It is the companion of a picture made two years earlier, Quiet Abode. The canvas hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

title: The Vladimirka
about: A worn dirt road runs straight across the plain to the horizon under a grey sky. This was the Vladimirka, the highway eastward from Moscow, along which for generations prisoners in chains were marched on foot to exile in Siberia. Levitan came upon it by chance while out hunting in the summer of 1892 and recognised what it was. He put no convicts in his picture; a lone pilgrim and a wayside shrine are enough. He did not sell the canvas but presented it himself to the Tretyakov Gallery, where it hangs still.

title: March
about: The snow is still deep, but it has begun to sink and turn blue in the shadows, and water drips from the roof of the porch. A shaggy horse waits before the door with a sledge, dozing in the first warm sun of the year. Levitan painted the picture in a single month, March of 1895, on a country estate in the Tver region, working outdoors in the thaw. A birdhouse hangs high in the bare birch. Generations of Russian landscape painters learned from this small canvas how to paint spring light upon snow. Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: Golden Autumn
about: Birches blaze yellow along a small dark river, and beyond them the fields are still green with winter wheat. Isaac Levitan painted the scene in 1895, in the countryside of the Tver region where he was staying. It is among the brightest of his works, a rare thing for a painter whose gift was for melancholy; he himself thought it somewhat coarse. He was a Jew in a hostile empire, twice ordered out of Moscow, and he died of a failing heart at thirty-nine. Pavel Tretyakov bought the picture the next year, and it hangs in his gallery.

title: The Lake. Rus
about: White clouds sail over a broad lake, and their shadows cross the water and the reeds. On the far shore lie villages, fields and white churches under the sun. This was Levitan's last great canvas, and he did not live to finish it. He worked on it through 1899 and into 1900, though his heart was failing, and he meant it for a summing up of all he had felt about his country; among his friends he called it simply Rus. He died that summer, not yet forty. The picture is in the Russian Museum, Saint Petersburg.

title: Above the Eternal Peace
about: A wooden chapel and a few leaning crosses stand upon a headland, and beneath them a great lake spreads away under piled storm clouds. A single window is lit. Levitan painted the canvas in 1894 from studies made at Lake Udomlya, north-west of Moscow, and he worked upon it, by his own account, to the sound of Beethoven's funeral march. In a letter to Pavel Tretyakov he said that he was wholly in this picture, with all his soul and all his being. Tretyakov bought it, and it remains in the gallery that bears his name.

title: Evening. Golden Plyos
about: Plyos is a small town on a high bank of the Volga, and Levitan spent three summers there, beginning in 1888. They were the happiest and most fruitful seasons of his short life. In this canvas of 1889 the sun has just gone down; a soft golden mist lies upon the river, and a white church and its bell tower stand out against the wooded hill. The house with the red roof near the water is one in which he rented rooms. The painting is in the Tretyakov Gallery, and Plyos keeps a museum in his memory.

title: Walk on the Beach
about: The painter's wife Clotilde and their elder daughter Maria walk along the shore at Valencia in the late afternoon, their white dresses and veils blown by the breeze off the sea. Joaquin Sorolla painted them in the summer of 1909, lately returned from a triumphant exhibition in New York, and at the height of his powers. He has cut off the top of Clotilde's hat and left out the horizon entirely, as a camera might. The whites are full of blue, violet and gold. The canvas has stayed in his own house in Madrid, which is now his museum.

title: The Return from Fishing
about: On the beach at Valencia the fishing boats were hauled ashore by yoked oxen, wading breast-deep in the surf. Joaquin Sorolla, who was born in that city and orphaned in infancy, painted the scene in 1894 on a canvas more than three metres wide. The great lateen sail, filled with wind and sun, takes up half the picture, and the water is alive with reflected light. He sent the work to the Paris Salon of 1895, where it won a medal and was bought by the French state. It made his name abroad. Musée d'Orsay.

title: Snapshot, Biarritz
about: The painter's wife, Clotilde, sits on the sand at Biarritz in the summer of 1906, veiled in white against the wind, and in her hands she holds a small folding camera, then the newest of pastimes. Sorolla set her down with a few swift strokes, as though the picture too had been taken in an instant. He had reason to honour photography; as a youth he had worked in the studio of a Valencian photographer, whose daughter Clotilde was. The canvas has never left the family house in Madrid, now the Museo Sorolla.

title: Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams
about: An empty room, a closed door and a window through which the sun slants to the floor. That is all, and Vilhelm Hammershøi needed no more. He painted the picture in 1900 in the apartment at Strandgade 30 in Copenhagen, where he and his wife Ida lived for ten years, and where he made more than sixty interiors. He had the walls and woodwork painted in greys and whites and removed nearly all the furniture. The light is solid enough to touch. The canvas belongs to the Ordrupgaard museum north of Copenhagen.

title: Interior in Strandgade, Sunlight on the Floor
about: A woman in black sits at a table with her back turned, and beside her the sun comes through a tall window and lays its pattern of panes on the bare boards. Hammershøi painted the room in 1901 in his apartment at Strandgade 30, in an old merchant's house in Copenhagen. The woman is his wife, Ida, and what she is doing is not told. The white door is shut. Everything here is grey, white and brown, and yet the picture is full of light. It hangs in the national gallery of Denmark.

title: Interior with Young Woman Seen from the Back
about: Ida Hammershøi stands before a grey wall with a tray held against her hip, and nothing is shown but the nape of her neck, her dark dress and the knot of her hair. On the sideboard beside her is a porcelain bowl whose lid does not sit quite true. Her husband painted the picture about 1904. He admired Vermeer and the Dutch masters of the quiet room, and went further than they in leaving things out. He spoke little, travelled reluctantly, and died at fifty-one. The canvas is in the art museum of Randers in Jutland.

title: Evening in Ukraine
about: The sun has dropped behind the hill, and its last rays turn the whitewashed walls of the cottages to rose and crimson, while the shadows upon them go a cold blue-green. Arkhip Kuindzhi showed the canvas in 1878, and it astonished and divided the public; some thought the colours impossible. He had observed that warm light makes cool shadow, and he pressed the contrast as far as paint would go. He returned to the picture and reworked it in 1901. It hangs in the Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg.

title: Birch Grove
about: Sunlight falls into a clearing among white birch trunks, and a green stream winds through the grass toward the dark wall of the forest. Arkhip Kuindzhi painted it in 1879. He was the son of a poor Greek shoemaker from Mariupol on the Sea of Azov, and largely taught himself. He simplified what he saw into flat patches of brilliant light and deep shadow, cutting off the trees at the top like a stage set, and the public was astonished by the force of the sun in it. The canvas hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery.

title: Red Sunset on the Dnieper
museum: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
about: In 1882, at the height of his fame, Kuindzhi ceased to exhibit, and for some twenty years the public saw nothing new from his hand. He went on painting in private and gave himself to his pupils. This large canvas belongs to those late years, between 1905 and 1908. The sun burns low through a bank of cloud and sets the whole sky and the wide river aflame, while a few thatched roofs lie dark on the near bank. He died in 1910 and left his fortune to a society for the support of artists. Metropolitan Museum, New York.

title: Hip, Hip, Hurrah!
about: At Skagen, the fishing village at the northern tip of Denmark, a colony of painters gathered each summer in the 1880s. After a garden party at the house of Michael and Anna Ancher in 1884, Peder Severin Krøyer began this picture of the friends on their feet with raised glasses. It took him four years to complete, with sitters coming and going. Sunlight filters through the leaves upon the white cloth and the bottles. The little girl is the Anchers' daughter, Helga. A Swedish collector bought the canvas and gave it to the museum at Gothenburg.

title: Summer Evening on Skagen's Southern Beach
about: Two women in white walk away along the edge of the sea, in that hour of the northern summer when the light goes blue and sky and water can hardly be told apart. They are the painter Anna Ancher and Marie Krøyer, the artist's wife. Krøyer conceived the picture after a dinner party in 1892, when the guests strolled down to the shore, and painted it the following year with the help of photographs. The people of Skagen call this time of evening the blue hour. The canvas is in the Skagens Museum.

title: Summer Evening at Skagen Beach - The Artist and His Wife
about: Krøyer walks beside his wife Marie on the sand at Skagen in the blue dusk of a summer night, with their dog at his heel and the moon laying a pale track on the sea. He painted the canvas in 1899 for his patron, the tobacco manufacturer Heinrich Hirschsprung. It appears a picture of contentment, and it was not so. The painter's mind had begun to fail, and within a few years Marie would leave him. They walk arm in arm, and he looks straight ahead. The picture hangs in the Hirschsprung Collection in Copenhagen.

title: Roses
about: In the garden of the house they rented at Skagen, Marie Krøyer sits reading in a deck chair beneath a great bush of white roses in full flower. The dog Rap sleeps at her feet, and a second chair stands empty for the painter. Krøyer painted the picture in the summer of 1893, four years after their marriage, when Marie was twenty-six and was spoken of as the most beautiful woman in Denmark. The blossoms fill almost half the canvas. It is on view at the Skagens Museum.

title: Fishermen Hauling a Net on Skagen's North Beach
about: A line of fishermen in oilskins and sea boots leans back upon a rope and draws the heavy net up out of the surf, in the low sun of a late afternoon. Krøyer had come to Skagen for the first time the year before, already an admired painter in Copenhagen and Paris, and he painted this large canvas in 1883. In those first seasons his subject was the labour of the fishing people. The blue evenings and white dresses for which he is loved came afterwards. The picture is in the Skagens Museum.

title: Reflections on the Thames, Westminster
about: John Atkinson Grimshaw was a railway clerk in Leeds who taught himself to paint, to the dismay of his devout parents. Moonlight became his province. In this canvas of 1880 the full moon stands over the Thames and the lit clock of Westminster, and a solitary woman pauses at the parapet of the new Embankment with a dog beside her. Whistler, who painted the same river by night, is reported to have said that he thought himself the inventor of nocturnes until he saw Grimshaw's moonlit pictures. Leeds Art Gallery.

title: Evening Glow
museum: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
about: A suburban lane runs between high garden walls, strewn with fallen leaves, and the bare trees stand black against an amber sky. A single woman with a basket has paused beside the wall. Grimshaw painted many such autumn evenings, and this one dates from 1884. He lived in an old manor house on the edge of Leeds and found his poetry in damp, smoke and gaslight, where other painters saw none. He left no letters or journals, and his pictures must speak for him. It is at the Yale Center for British Art.

title: The Poor Poet
about: In a garret under the tiles a poet lies in bed in his nightcap, with an umbrella hung open above him against the leaking roof. He counts out the metre of a verse upon his fingers, and his own manuscripts wait beside the stove to be burned for warmth. Carl Spitzweg, a Munich apothecary who had taught himself to paint, showed the picture in 1839, and the critics of his city were not amused. It has since become one of the best-loved paintings in Germany. This version hangs in the Neue Pinakothek, Munich.

title: The Sunday Stroll
about: A respectable family walks out in single file through a field of ripe corn on a hot Sunday. The father goes first, stout and perspiring, and has hung his tall hat upon his walking stick to shade himself; his wife and children follow behind with their parasols. Spitzweg painted the scene in 1841. He looked upon the townsfolk of his day with affection and a little mischief, and never mocked them cruelly. He is the chief painter of that comfortable and narrow world the Germans call Biedermeier. Salzburg Museum.

title: Midsummer Dance
about: It is past midnight on the eve of Saint John, and the young people of the village are still dancing in the yard, in the grey light that serves the Swedish summer for darkness. The first sun strikes the gable of the red house and the top of the maypole. Anders Zorn painted the scene in 1897 at Mora in Dalarna, the country district where he was born a brewery maid's son and to which he returned a rich and celebrated man. The maypole was his own gift to the village. Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.

title: Lake Keitele
about: Bands of silver cross the still water of a lake in central Finland, where the wind has ruffled the surface and left the rest a mirror for the clouds. Akseli Gallen-Kallela stayed beside Lake Keitele in the summer of 1904, recovering from an illness, and made four versions of the view. He was the foremost painter of his nation, then under Russian rule, and the illustrator of its epic, the Kalevala; the streaks have been read as the wake of the hero Väinämöinen's boat. This canvas of 1905 was bought by the National Gallery in 1999.

title: Moscow Courtyard
about: In the summer of 1877 Vasily Polenov, lately returned from years of study in Paris, took lodgings in a quiet lane near the Arbat in Moscow. This was the view from his window: a grassy yard with a well and a sagging barn, children playing, a woman carrying a bucket, a horse waiting in harness, and beyond the roofs the white bell tower and five domes of a church. He painted it in 1878 and sent it to the exhibition of the Wanderers, half apologising for so slight a subject. It was loved at once. Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

title: Overgrown Pond
about: In a corner of an old park the water lies dark and still beneath the trees, half covered with lily pads, and a small plank jetty runs out from the bank. Look into the shade beneath the trees and a woman in a pale dress may be found, seated on a bench and lost in thought. Vasily Polenov painted the picture in 1879, the year after his Moscow Courtyard, and showed it with the Wanderers. It has the same tenderness for quiet, neglected places. It hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

title: Breakfast under the Big Birch
about: The whole family sits at a long table in the garden, in the shade of a great birch, and the dog has taken a place on the bench among the children. Carl Larsson had grown up in the poorest quarter of Stockholm. In 1888 his wife's father gave the couple a small cottage at Sundborn in Dalarna, and they made of it, room by room, the most famous home in Sweden. He painted this watercolour in 1896 and published it with others in a book called A Home. The series belongs to the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.

title: Flowers on the Windowsill
about: A girl in a pinafore waters the pot plants that crowd the sill of a wide, bright window. This is the drawing room of the Larssons' cottage at Sundborn, and the child is their eldest daughter, Suzanne. The summer of 1894 was so wet that the painter could not work out of doors; his wife Karin suggested that he draw the rooms of the house instead. So began the watercolours that carried the Swedish home, with its light walls and plain painted furniture, across the world. Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
